ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY

40 CFR Part 52

[EPA-R09-OAR-2026-5581; FRL-13513-01-R9]


Air Quality Plan; Arizona; Pinal County Air Quality Control 
District; West Pinal County PM10 Nonattainment Area; Fugitive Dust 
Rules

AGENCY: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

ACTION: Proposed rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to 
approve revisions to the Pinal County Air Quality Control District 
(PCAQCD or ``District'') portion of the Arizona State Implementation 
Plan (SIP). These revisions concern emissions of particulate matter 
(PM) that is 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter (PM10) 
from fugitive dust sources, including open areas/vacant lots, unpaved 
lots, unpaved roads, paved public roadways, and construction sites. We 
are proposing to approve local rules to regulate these emission sources 
under the Clean Air Act (CAA or ``Act'').

[[Page 66045]]

B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?

    We are proposing this action under section 110 of the CAA. Pursuant 
to CAA section 110(a), States are required to submit SIPs to the EPA 
that provide for the implementation, maintenance, and enforcement of 
the national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS). CAA section 110(k) 
requires SIPs to meet certain procedural requirements and requires the 
EPA to approve or disapprove SIP submissions. CAA section 110(l) 
requires States to provide public notice and an opportunity for public 
hearing of SIP revisions prior to their submittal and prohibits the EPA 
from approving any SIP revisions that would interfere with attainment 
or maintenance of a NAAQS, reasonable further progress, or other 
applicable requirements of the CAA. If a SIP submittal meets all the 
applicable CAA requirements, then the EPA must approve the submittal 
under CAA section 110(k)(3).
    For this submittal to be approved, we must consider CAA 
requirements related to the emissions limitations in the submitted 
rules. CAA sections 110(a)(2)(A) and 302(k) require emissions 
limitations in the SIP to be enforceable and continuous, respectively. 
CAA section 172(c)(6) requires SIPs for nonattainment areas ``include 
enforceable emissions limitations, and such other control measures 
means or techniques . . . as well as schedules and timetables for 
compliance, as may be necessary or appropriate to provide for 
attainment of such standard in such area by the applicable attainment 
date . . . .'' Also, 40 CFR part 51, subpart K, requires SIPs to 
contain legally enforceable procedures for monitoring the status of 
compliance with the requirements in the control strategy. Finally, 
while these rules were submitted to meet BACM requirements under CAA 
section 189(b)(1)(B) and MSM requirements under CAA section 188(e), we 
are not evaluating them for BACM or MSM in this rulemaking action. We 
will evaluate BACM and MSM in a separate Federal Register notice in the 
context of the broader attainment plan action for the West Pinal County 
PM10 nonattainment area.
    We are proposing that this submittal meets all applicable CAA 
requirements and are proposing to fully approve it under CAA section 
110(k)(3).

II. Background

A. PM10 NAAQS

    The EPA establishes the NAAQS for certain ambient air pollutants at 
levels required to protect public health and welfare. Emissions of 
PM10 contribute to effects that are harmful to human health 
and the environment, including premature mortality, aggravation of 
respiratory and cardiovascular disease, decreased lung function, 
visibility impairment, and damage to vegetation and ecosystems. 
Accordingly, the EPA revised the NAAQS for particulate matter on July 
1, 1987, replacing the standards for total suspended particulates, 
which are particles 30 micrometers or smaller in diameter, with new 
standards applying only to PM10.\1\ In revising the NAAQS 
for particulate matter, we established a 24-hour standard of 150 
micrograms per cubic meter ([micro]g/m\3\), as well as an annual 
standard that was subsequently revoked in 2006.\2\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ 52 FR 24634 (Jul. 1, 1987).
    \2\ 71 FR 61144 (Oct. 17, 2006).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. Area Description

    On May 31, 2012, the EPA designated a portion of state lands in 
western Pinal County, Arizona, as nonattainment for the 1987 
p.m.10 NAAQS.\3\ The West Pinal County PM10 
nonattainment area encompasses approximately 1,325 square miles lying 
within a basin characterized by low desert valleys between the Phoenix 
and Tucson metropolitan areas. It includes all or portions of the 
incorporated cities and towns of Apache Junction, Casa Grande, 
Coolidge, Eloy, Florence, Queen Creek, and Maricopa, with a population 
of approximately 343,788 based upon July 1, 2017 U.S. Census Bureau 
data. Average elevation in the nonattainment area is 1,403 feet above 
sea level, with elevations of up to 6,441 feet directly east of the 
nonattainment area, which becomes more mountainous.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \3\ 77 FR 32024 (May 31, 2012). The boundaries for the West 
Pinal County nonattainment area are described in 40 CFR 81.303.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The West Pinal County PM10 nonattainment area was 
originally classified as ``Moderate'' nonattainment on May 31, 2012, 
with an attainment date of December 31, 2018. CAA section 188(b)(2) 
requires the EPA to determine whether a PM10 nonattainment 
area classified as Moderate has attained the 1987 24-hour 
PM10 NAAQS by the area's attainment date. If the EPA 
determines that a Moderate area has not attained the NAAQS by the 
relevant attainment date, then the area shall be reclassified as a 
Serious area by operation of law. On June 24, 2020, we took final 
action to determine that the West Pinal County PM10 
nonattainment area did not attain the 1987 24-hour PM10 
NAAQS, and as a result, it was reclassified to Serious nonattainment by 
operation of law.\4\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \4\ 85 FR 37756 (Jun. 24, 2020).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

IV. The EPA's Evaluation of Arizona's Submittal

A. How is the EPA evaluating the submittal?

    Emission limitations in the SIP must be enforceable, continuous, 
and must not interfere with applicable requirements concerning 
attainment and reasonable further progress or other CAA 
requirements.\9\ Additionally, 40 CFR part 51, subpart K, requires SIPs 
to have enforceable procedures for monitoring the status of compliance 
with the requirements in the control strategy.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \9\ See, CAA sections 110(a)(2), 302(k) and 110(l), 
respectively.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The PCAQCD regulates a PM10 nonattainment area 
classified as Serious for the 1987 24-hour PM10 NAAQS. In 
Serious nonattainment areas, SIPs must implement BACM, including Best 
Available Control Technology.\10\ In addition, because Arizona is 
seeking a five-year extension of the attainment date, the SIP must also 
implement MSM.\11\ These evaluations are included in the context of the 
broader attainment plan rulemaking and are not included in this 
rulemaking. In this rulemaking, we are evaluating these rules for 
approval into the SIP under CAA section 110 requirements.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \10\ CAA section 189(b)(1)(B).
    \11\ CAA section 188(e).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Our evaluation also relies on relevant guidance and policy 
documents to evaluate enforceability and revisions/relaxation 
requirements.\12\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \12\ See, ``State Implementation Plans; General Preamble for the 
Implementation of Title I of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990,'' 
57 FR 13498 (Apr. 16, 1992); 57 FR 18070 (Apr. 28, 1992); ``Guidance 
Document for Correcting Common VOC & Other Rule Deficiencies,'' EPA 
Region 9, August 21, 2001 (the Little Bluebook); ``State 
Implementation Plans for Serious PM-10 Nonattainment Areas, and

and ``Fugitive Dust Background Document and Technical Information 
Document for Best Available Control Measures,'' EPA 450/2-92-004, 
September 1992.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. Do the submittals meet the evaluation criteria?

    We evaluated these rules to ensure they meet CAA requirements and 
are consistent with relevant guidance regarding enforceability and SIP 
revisions.
1. Article 1 Rules
    Article 1 applies to ``non-traditional'' fugitive dusts sources in 
the West Pinal County PM10 nonattainment area: open areas/
vacant lots, vehicle use in open areas/vacant lots, unpaved lots, weed 
abatement and/or trash removal, unpaved roads, and paved public 
roadways. Affected owners and operators are required to implement 
control measures that will meet visible emission and surface 
stabilization standards. Compliance with stabilization and visible 
emission standards are determined through applicable test methods in 
Article 9.
    Each of the regulated activities has specific standards and control 
measures that must be met. For visible emission standards, either a 20 
percent opacity limit applies or visible emissions, including fugitive 
dust, are prohibited from going beyond the property line. Owners and 
operators choose the stabilization standard they will meet from a list 
of options, such as maintaining a soil crust, meeting a minimum 
threshold friction velocity (TFV) \13\ limit, covering the area with a 
certain percentage of vegetative cover, or meeting silt loading \14\ 
limits. Owners and operators then choose a control measure to implement 
for each regulated activity from a menu of options, such as 
establishing vegetative cover, applying dust suppressants, applying 
water, restoring the area to an undisturbed native condition, 
establishing barriers to prevent unauthorized vehicle access, paving 
parking lots, and applying and maintaining surface gravel. 
Additionally, disturbed surface areas of 0.10 acres (4,356 square feet) 
or greater must sign up to receive the Pinal County Dust Control 
Forecast and ensure control measures are implemented on the day prior 
and day of a high dust risk forecast.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \13\ TFV relates to a material's susceptibility to erosion from 
wind. Materials with a higher TFV are less susceptible to wind 
erosion and are associated with lower fugitive dust emissions.
    \14\ ``Silt'' refers to aggregate material (dirt, sand, rock) 
that has a particle size of 75 micrometers or less. ``Silt loading'' 
refers to the concentration of silt on unpaved surfaces. Higher silt 
loading, that is, higher concentrations of smaller particles, is 
associated with higher fugitive dust emissions.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Article 1 includes a new standard for paving existing unpaved 
roadways. Beginning January 1, 2024, each city, county, or state agency 
with primary responsibility for any existing unpaved road within the 
West Pinal County PM10 nonattainment area was required to 
annually pave an average of 20 percent of unpaved roads within the 
agency's jurisdiction.\15\ Further, if the EPA determines the West 
Pinal County PM10 nonattainment area failed to make 
reasonable further progress, or to attain the PM10 NAAQS by 
the attainment date, the rules include a contingency measure where any 
public unpaved road with average daily trips of 26 or more will have a 
speed limit of 15 miles per hour.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \15\ Up to a maximum of 5 cumulative miles for each agency.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For paved public roads, Article 1 establishes new standards by 
requiring street sweeping to be done by certified street sweepers and 
establishing paved road development standards that specify minimum 
surface stabilization standards for road shoulders.
    Each person subject to Article 1 is required to compile and retain 
records that provide evidence of control measure application (i.e., 
receipts and/or purchase records). The records must describe the type 
of treatment or control measure, extent of coverage, and date applied. 
Records must be available to the District upon request and maintained 
for at least two years. Agencies subject to the road paving requirement 
must submit annual progress reports by January 30 of each year related 
to the annual road paving requirements and the number of paved roads 
with unpaved shoulders.
    Overall, the visible emission limits, stabilization standards, and 
control measures are tailored to minimizing fugitive dust from each 
type of regulated activity, result in continuous emissions limitations, 
and the associated recordkeeping and reporting requirements are 
sufficient to meet the enforceability requirements of CAA sections 
110(a)(2)(A) and 172(c)(6) and 40 CFR part 51, subpart K. The 
amendments strengthen the existing SIP, consistent with CAA section 
110(l), by expanding existing control measures, such as lowering 
applicability thresholds, adding or revising visible emission 
standards, establishing clear timelines for when control measures must 
be implemented, clarifying that control measures are considered to be 
implemented when the associated visible emission and/or stabilization 
standards are met, and adding new control measures for paved and 
unpaved roads. Because they meet all applicable CAA requirements, we 
propose approving the rules from Article 1 into the Arizona SIP.
2. Article 3 Rules
    Article 3 applies to fugitive dusts sources at construction sites 
within the

[[Page 66047]]

West Pinal County PM10 nonattainment area. Affected owners 
and operators are required to implement control measures and meet 
visible emission standards and surface stabilization standards for dust 
generating activities. Additionally, owners or operators are required 
to obtain a dust permit when dust-generating operations at construction 
sites disturb a total surface area of 0.10 acres (4,356 square feet) or 
more. All permit applications must contain a dust control plan that 
identifies all control measures to be implemented before, after, and 
while conducting any dust-generating operation.
    Sites with a dust control permit must: for each project of 5 or 
more acres, have a project information sign that identifies how the 
public can file a dust complaint to the District; meet dust control 
training requirements once every three years from the District; except 
in certain high wind conditions, implement all control measures 
necessary to maintain soil stability; implement control measures 
specified for each type of activity, such as active areas, demolition, 
weed abatement, trackout, site grade preparation, trenching, and haul 
roads; limit dust generated on the property to 20 percent opacity, and 
ensure no visible emissions, including fugitive dust, go beyond the 
property line; install no trespassing signs for project sites when 
activities cease for 30 or more days at a time; and, on a high dust 
risk day, continue to implement control measures that maintain 
compliance with the applicable standards or cease dust-generating 
activities and ensure disturbed surface areas are stablized for the 
day. Construction sites that do not require a dust control permit are 
subject to the same general control measures, visible emission 
standards, and stabilization requirements but are not subject to 
signage and dust control training requirements. Similar to Article 1, 
owners and operators subject to Article 3 choose from a menu of options 
to meet control measure requirements and surface stabilization 
standards.
    Any person who conducts dust-generating operations that require a 
dust control permit is required to keep written records of self-
inspection on each day dust-generating operations are conducted. Self-
inspection records include daily inspections for crusted or damp soil, 
trackout conditions and clean-up measures, daily water usage for dust 
control measures, and dust suppressant application. Any person who 
conducts dust-generating operations that do not require a dust control 
permit must maintain records that provide evidence of control measure 
application, by indicating the type of treatment or control measure, 
extent of coverage, and date applied. Records are required to be 
maintained for two years, except for construction sites at a facility 
with a title V operating permit, which must maintain records for five 
years.
    Overall, the dust control permit requirements, visible emission 
limits, stabilization standards, and control measures are tailored to 
minimizing fugitive dust for each type of regulated activity, result in 
continuous emission limitations, and associated recordkeeping 
requirements are sufficient to meet the enforceability requirements of 
CAA sections 110(a)(2)(A) and 172(c)(6) and 40 CFR part 51, subpart K. 
The amendments would strengthen the existing SIP in several ways, 
consistent with CAA section 110(l), including adding a visible emission 
standard that prohibits visible emissions from going beyond the 
property line, adding signage requirements and dust control operator 
training requirements, specifying the threshold for obtaining a dust 
control permit, specifying the dust generating activities that are 
required to implement control measures, specifying the types of control 
measures that apply to each type of dust generating activity, 
specifying that control measures must be implemented at all times, and 
requiring daily records of actions to reduce fugitive dust. Because 
they meet all applicable CAA requirements, we are proposing to approve 
the rules from Article 3 into the Arizona SIP.
3. Rescission of Section 4-3-190
    Previously, if certain conditions were met, Section 4-3-190 
provided an exemption from the requirements of Article 3 during high 
wind conditions and emergency maintenance of flood control channels and 
water retention basins. The rule amendments adopted by the District to 
Article 3 on January 25, 2023, incorporate requirements that apply 
during these circumstances within other provisions of Article 3 such 
that removal of this section would not relax any existing SIP 
requirement and is consistent with CAA section 110(l).\16\ Therefore, 
we are proposing to approve this rescission request.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \16\ See, Section 4-3-180.I.2.b, contains required control 
measures during high wind events, Section 4-3-170.20, adds a 
definition for ``high wind conditions,'' and Section 4-3-160.A.5.i 
is a comparable exemption for emergency maintenance of flood control 
channels, conditioned on implementation of all permitted control 
measures.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

4. Article 9 Rules
    Section 4-9-310 establishes test methods to determine whether 
unpaved shoulders and medians of paved roads meet applicable surface 
stabilization standards. It includes an opacity test method, silt 
loading test method, and gravel depth and silt content test method. 
These test methods are used to determine compliance with stabilization 
standards in Article 1 and 3.
    Based upon our evaluation, these test methods are enforceable and 
consistent with comparable test methods established in Federal 
requirements and SIP-approved fugitive dust rules in other States. We 
consider their use with Articles 1 and 3 to be an appropriate 
application of the test methods. The test methods ensure the associated 
emission limits will meet the enforceability requirements of CAA 
sections 110(a)(2)(A) and 172(c)(6) and 40 CFR part 51, subpart K, 
strengthen the SIP, and would not interfere with any other CAA 
requirements, consistent with CAA section 110(l). Because the rule 
meets all applicable CAA requirements, we are proposing to approve 
Section 4-9-310 into the Arizona SIP.
    As stated above in section III.B, the EPA is not acting on Sections 
4-9-320 and 4-9-340 from the state's submittal in this action. These 
rules are already approved into the SIP and PCAQCD has not amended them 
locally, so no further action is needed.
5. Conclusions
    Based on our review, the rules proposed for approval, as listed in 
Table 1 of this document, and the proposed rescission of Section 4-3-
190 meet the relevant CAA requirements. The technical support documents 
(TSDs) for each article (Articles 1, 3, and 9) have more information on 
our evaluation and are available in the docket for this rulemaking.

C. Proposed Action and Public Comment

    As authorized in section 110(k)(3) of the Act, the EPA proposes to 
approve Arizona's February 13, 2023 SIP submittal, including approving 
the rules listed in Table 1 of this document into the Pinal County 
portion of the Arizona SIP and the rescission of Section 4-3-190 from 
the SIP, because they fulfill all relevant requirements. We will accept 
comments from the public on this proposal until November 18, 2026. If 
finalized as proposed, our final action will incorporate the rules 
listed in Table 1 of this document into the federally enforceable SIP 
and Section 4-3-190 will be removed from the SIP.

January 25, 2023, which regulate fugitive dust emissions from open 
areas/vacant lots, unpaved lots, weed abatement, unpaved roads, and 
paved public roadways in the West Pinal County Serious PM10 
Nonattainment Area. The EPA is also proposing to incorporate by 
reference PCAQD, Code of Regulations, Chapter 4, Article 3, Sections 4-
3-160, ``General Provisions--West Pinal PM10 Nonattainment 
Area;'' 4-3-170, ``Definitions;'' and 4-3-180 ``Dust Generating 
Operations: Standards, Application, Permit, Recordkeeping and Training 
Requirements'' as amended on January 25, 2023, which regulate fugitive 
dust emissions from construction sites in the West Pinal County Serious 
PM10 Nonattainment Area. The EPA is also proposing to 
incorporate by reference PCAQD, Code of Regulations, Chapter 4, Article 
9, Section 4-9-310, ``Test Methods for Stabilization for Unpaved 
Shoulders and Medians of Paved Roads,'' as adopted on January 25, 2023, 
which establishes test methods used to determine compliance with 
requirements for dust generating activities contained in PCAQD, Code of 
Regulations, Chapter 4, Articles 1 and 3. The EPA has made, and will 
continue to make, these materials available through https://www.regulations.gov and at the EPA Region IX Office (please contact the 
person identified in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section of 
this preamble for more information).

VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews

    Under the CAA, the Administrator is required to approve a SIP 
submission that complies with the provisions of the Act and applicable 
federal regulations. 42 U.S.C. 7410(k); 40 CFR 52.02(a). Thus, in 
reviewing SIP submissions, the EPA's role is to approve state choices, 
provided that they meet the criteria of the CAA. Accordingly, this 
proposed action merely proposes to approve state law as meeting federal 
requirements and does not impose additional requirements beyond those 
imposed by state law. For that reason, this proposed action:
     Is not a significant regulatory action subject to review 
by the Office of Management and Budget under Executive Order 12866 (58 
FR 51735, October 4, 1993);
     Is not an Executive Order 14192 (90 FR 9065, February 6, 
2025) regulatory action because this action is not significant under 
Executive Order 12866;
     Does not impose an information collection burden under the 
provisions of the Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq.);
     Is certified as not having a significant economic impact 
on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory 
Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.);
     Does not contain any unfunded mandate or significantly or 
uniquely affect small governments, as described in the Unfunded 
Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (Pub. L. 104-4);
     Does not have federalism implications as specified in 
Executive Order 13132 (64 FR 43255, August 10, 1999);
     Is not subject to Executive Order 13045 (62 FR 19885, 
April 23, 1997) because it proposes to approve a state program;
     Is not a significant regulatory action subject to 
Executive Order 13211 (66 FR 28355, May 22, 2001); and
     Is not subject to requirements of section 12(d) of the 
National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (15 U.S.C. 272 
note) because application of those requirements would be inconsistent 
with the CAA.
    In addition, the SIP is not approved to apply on any Indian 
reservation land or in any other area where the EPA or an Indian Tribe 
has demonstrated that a Tribe has jurisdiction. In those areas of 
Indian country, the rule does not have Tribal implications and will not 
impose substantial direct costs on Tribal governments or preempt Tribal 
law as specified by Executive Order 13175 (65 FR 67249, November 9, 
2000).
